title: Hell in the Torah
hook: If eternal hellfire is real, why does the Torah never mention it?
tldr: The Bible speaks in metaphor, parable and narrative, and reading figures of speech literally creates hellfire. The Hebrew Scriptures have no word for hellfire; Sheol simply means the grave. The Torah is a narrative serving as Israel's constitution, with earthly consequences: restitution, fines, even physical death, but never eternal torment for breaking a commandment.
big_idea: The Torah's penalties were earthly; it never threatens eternal hellfire.

points.title: Figures of speech, not forecasts
points.text: Like 'financial meltdown' or a coach saying 'we grilled them', Jesus' darkness and fire imagery used familiar figures. He said he spoke figuratively and in parables.

points.title: Christianity cut from its roots
points.text: Constantine and the Council of Nicaea severed Christianity from Judaism, excluding Jewish bishops and replacing Passover and Sabbath, which left Jesus and Paul misread as non-Jewish teachers.

points.title: Sheol means the grave
points.text: Jacob said he would go down to Sheol to his son. Translating it 'hell' makes no sense; in Judaism Sheol is where all the dead rest until judgment day.

points.title: The Torah is a narrative
points.text: Laws are a small part of a story that functioned as Israel's constitution, promising earthly blessings, not a manual for escaping hellfire.

points.title: Penalties were earthly
points.text: Theft meant restitution of four sheep for one; even capital crimes brought physical death. No prophet, king or judge tied commandments to eternal life or hellfire.

points.title: Sin starts in the mind
points.text: Jesus' teaching that lust is adultery in the heart warns that private thoughts lead to public actions, not that a glance earns eternal torture.

sections.h: Figures of speech we all understand
sections.summary: Nobody pictures Wall Street skyscrapers melting at a 'financial meltdown', politicians in armor on a 'political battlefield', managers hunting staff in a 'corporate jungle', or journalists dressed as bees in a 'media circus'. Mostly illiterate ancient societies relied even more on metaphors, stories and parables. A coach texting 'we grilled the Yankees, I can still smell the smoke' would be absurd if read literally in 4025; modern Bible readers make that same genre mistake.

Jewish teachers always used figurative language, metaphor and analogy, as did the rabbis Jesus and Paul. 'I am the bread of life' does not make Jesus pastry; 'you are the light of the world' is not about candles. Paul's 'God's field, God's building' and 'the full armor of God' are not soil or iron. Ignoring these devices loses the text's richness and can produce superficial, misinformed or even harmful interpretations.

Emperor Constantine (4th century) uprooted Christianity from Judaism: removing Jewish priests, inserting pagan practices, declaring 'nothing in common with the detestable Jewish crowd'. The Council of Nicaea (325, Turkey) barred bishops of Jewish background and replaced First Fruits and Passover with Easter and Saturday Sabbath with Sunday. Quartodecimans, who kept Passover on 14 Nisan, were persecuted; circumcision became a capital crime; Jews lost office, residence, business and travel rights.

Hell is pictured as utter darkness yet a lake of searing fire, with eternal torture, gnashing teeth and tears, though fire gives light. Jesus' Jewish audience heard proverbial figures; he said he spoke figuratively and in parables. Taking 'drinks my blood' literally would limit life to a few and break the Law's ban on eating blood, which Jesus came to fulfill. Few literally gouge out eyes or cut off hands, though those verses mention Gehenna.

By the first English translations, the hellfire tradition was so ingrained that it shaped how translators handled 'Gehenna', causing many of today's misconceptions. The Bible is a narrative using metaphor, parable and allegory, not a textbook. The Augustinian-Calvinist view reads hyperbole, parables and allegory literally. This part examines the passages ECT advocates cite most, by 'Sufficient Sampling' or 'Representative Refutation': refuting a representative sample, such as 20 verses, demonstrates the point.

sections.h: Sheol: the realm of the dead
sections.summary: The Hebrew Scriptures have no term for hellfire; Sheol is the realm of the dead, like a grave. Mourning Joseph, Jacob said he would go down to Sheol to his son; the NIV says 'grave'. The Douay-Rheims 'into hell' makes no sense: why would Jacob want hell, or think his son burns there? English versions translate Sheol as grave, underworld, pit, death and hell, causing theological confusion. 'Hell' once meant something else.

John MacArthur claims hellfire goes back to Moses, citing the King James 'burns to the lowest part of hell'. But the Hebrew word is Sheol. The literal JPS reads 'a fire is kindled in My nostril, and burneth unto the depths of the nether-world'. Read literally, God has a nose shooting fire at mountains; in context it is a metaphor for God's wrath reaching even the underworld. Relying on one translation breeds confusion.

Without a hellfire concept in the Old Testament, Jewish afterlife views differ markedly from later Christianity. In Judaism Sheol is neutral, where all deceased souls rest until judgment day, not torment. Moses and the Prophets never described Sheol as torment; the Law of Moses focuses on temporal rewards and punishments. The Torah and Prophets stress immediate consequences within one's lifetime, not posthumous suffering or reward.

sections.h: Was Hellfire the Consequence of Breaking the Ten Commandments?
sections.summary: Ray Comfort's 'Ten Commandments Interrogation' videos, with about half a billion views, ask strangers if they have lied, stolen or lusted; nearly all have, from praising an ugly bridal dress to keeping a work pen. In an all-male Dallas Theological Seminary doctoral class, nobody denied lesbian fantasies. Comfort says you must be morally perfect or face the lake of fire; Paul Washer says our debt to God was eternal punishment.

sections.h: A lustful glance and eternal fire?
sections.summary: In August 2022 Comfort told a young Israeli Jew that his lustful looks, adultery per Matthew 5:28, meant hellfire; the man politely disagreed. The logic: God gives strong sexual instincts, then must eternally torture you for an inevitable thought, a path toward mandatory hijabs and legalism. It is like life in prison for illegal parking or cutting off a child's hand for porn, harsher than North Korea or Iran.

sections.h: What Jesus meant: thoughts become actions
sections.summary: The problem is not Jesus or the Law but tying the Law to eternal life or hellfire. If Matthew 5:28 were a literal death sentence (Leviticus 20:10), calling someone 'fool' would risk damnation too, making Jesus threaten torture for anything short of perfection. As a rabbi he taught figuratively. Every company starts as an idea, every shooting as a thought. Andy Woods: private thoughts lead to public actions, so guard the mind.

Torah means the Pentateuch and also its laws, a confusing term due to mistranslation. Its genre is narrative, one 'Book of Moses' later split into five; laws are a small fraction. Professor Simeon Chavel: the Torah is first a narrative, not a law book. Judaism sees its commandments as rites, customs, morals and justice for daily life, Israel's constitution, just as Americans do not see the U.S. Constitution as a path to eternal life.

sections.h: Laws for a nation's daily life
sections.summary: Deuteronomy 28 promises earthly blessings: city, country, womb, crops, livestock, barns. Like modern law the Torah regulates taxation, banking and labor; today it might ban smoking on planes or crossing on a red signal. Fines do not decide eternal fate. No prophet, king or judge linked commandments to eternal life or hellfire; that would have been alien to Israel. Penalties, even death, were physical, not spiritual or eternal.

If a hungry neighbor steals and eats a sheep, Exodus 22:1 requires four sheep in return, preferably chubby: restitution, not hellfire. A man who seized an unbetrothed virgin paid her father fifty shekels and had to provide for her for life. David stole, committed adultery with Bathsheba and arranged Uriah's murder; after about a year God sent Nathan, who announced punishment but never mentioned the afterlife or demanded David's resignation.

sections.h: The rebellious son: what kind of death?
sections.summary: The fifth commandment, honor your parents, carries the harshest penalty: whoever curses father or mother shall surely be put to death. What death: spiritual, or eternal fire? Deuteronomy 21 answers: the stubborn, rebellious, gluttonous son is brought to the elders and stoned by the men of the city. A physical death penalty might remove someone from society, but it was never linked to eternal punishment. Earthly behavior affects earthly life.

Nowhere does the Torah threaten eternal condemnation for breaking a commandment. The Pentateuch, foundation of all biblical theology, is silent on hell as eternal torment, which casts serious doubt on hellfire and suggests it is a later development. Comfort, Washer and others are sincere and zealous, but they distort God's character and the Good News, reducing sin to eternal damnation for coveting a neighbor's convertible and ignoring context and compassion.

mythfact.myth: Hellfire goes back to Moses, as Deuteronomy 32:22 says 'hell'.
mythfact.fact: The Hebrew word is Sheol, the realm of the dead; the verse is a metaphor of God's wrath, fire from his nostril reaching the underworld.

mythfact.myth: Breaking any of the Ten Commandments earns eternal torment in the lake of fire.
mythfact.fact: The Torah prescribes earthly consequences, like restitution or physical penalties; no prophet, king or judge linked commandments to eternal life or hellfire.

mythfact.myth: The Torah is a law book for getting saved.
mythfact.fact: Its genre is narrative; the laws, a small fraction, functioned as Israel's constitution governing earthly life, like the U.S. Constitution.

A grave offense brings a fine and lifelong provision, not damnation.

The death penalty for a rebellious son is physical stoning, not hellfire.
Obedience brings earthly blessings in the land: the Law concerns this life.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word Sheol most simply mean?
options: The realm of the dead, like a grave
quiz.why: Jacob expects to go down to Sheol to his son; the NIV renders it 'grave'. Judaism sees it as where all the dead rest.

quiz.q: Under Exodus 22:1, what happens to someone who steals and eats a sheep?
quiz.why: God's justice for theft is restitution: four sheep for a sheep, five oxen for an ox.

quiz.q: What did Nathan say about David's afterlife after Bathsheba and Uriah?
quiz.why: Nathan made no threat about the afterlife and God did not even demand David's resignation; both understood his afterlife was not at stake.

reflect: Why might the foundational books of the Bible say nothing about eternal hellfire if it were central to God's message?
